native_commit_info.subject: Testing balanced parentheses tree structure against main branch (#2637)
native_commit_info.body:
* ENH: add the balanced parentheses (BP) succinct tree backend (#2498)

* BLD: vendor the BitArray C library for the BP tree backend

Add the BitArray C sources (bit_array.c/.h, bit_macros.h) from
https://github.com/noporpoise/BitArray that the balanced-parentheses
(BP) tree backend compiles and links against. A .gitignore exception
keeps bit_array.c tracked despite the repository-wide *.c ignore rule,
since this source is vendored rather than generated by Cython.

* ENH: add the balanced parentheses (BP) succinct tree backend

Port the BP succinct tree data structure from improved-octo-waddle
(https://github.com/biocore/improved-octo-waddle) into a new
skbio.tree.bp subpackage. Add the core Cython modules: the succinct
structure itself (_bp), its Python bitarray wrapper (_ba), the
header-only binary-tree helpers (_bp_binary_tree), and the higher-level
Newick/jplace I/O (_bp_io), TreeNode conversion (_bp_conv), and
fully-resolved insertion (_bp_insert) modules.

* BLD: register the BP Cython extensions and expose the public API

Register the BP Cython extensions in setup.py and ship the BP test
fixtures as package data in pyproject.toml. Re-export the public BP
objects (BP, parse_newick, write_newick, parse_jplace, the TreeNode
converters, and insert_fully_resolved) from skbio.tree so they are
importable as part of the public API.

* TST: add tests and data for the BP tree backend

Add the BP test suite covering the succinct structure, Newick/jplace
I/O, TreeNode conversion, and insertion, including a Cython-level test
module (test_bp_cy) that exercises cdef methods unreachable from Python.

* API: rename the BP class to BPTree

Rename the balanced-parentheses tree class from ``BP`` to the more
descriptive ``BPTree`` across the Cython sources, the public
re-exports from skbio.tree, and the tests. Object representation and
pickling are updated to match. The module/file names and the "BP"
abbreviation used for the subpackage are left unchanged.

* API: rename the BPTree bit array attribute from B to data

Rename the public attribute that holds the parentheses bit array from
``B`` to ``data`` throughout the Cython sources and tests. The
constructor argument and the .npz serialization key remain ``B``, as
they are not part of the renamed attribute surface.

* DOC: document the BPTree API and surface it in the documentation

Add numpydoc docstrings for the BPTree methods (read, write, ntips,
collapse) and the BP I/O functions (parse_newick, write_newick,
parse_jplace), and describe the data attribute. Wire the BP public API
into the rendered docs with autosummary sections in skbio.tree and a
dedicated BPTree class template.

* API: align BPTree method names and docstrings with TreeNode

Rename BPTree's succinct-tree methods to scikit-bio's snake_case and
"tip" terminology, matching the equivalent or adjacent methods on
TreeNode:

  isleaf                 -> is_tip
  isancestor             -> is_ancestor
  fchild / lchild        -> first_child / last_child
  nsibling / psibling    -> next_sibling / previous_sibling
  deepestnode            -> deepest_node
  levelancestor          -> level_ancestor
  levelnext              -> level_next
  preorder / postorder   -> preorder_rank / postorder_rank
  preorderselect         -> preorder_select
  postorderselect        -> postorder_select
  subtree                -> subtree_size

Rewrite the affected docstrings in the numpydoc format used across
scikit-bio, cross-referencing the related TreeNode methods and noting
that these operations return integer indices or counts rather than
TreeNode objects. The depth and parent docstrings are brought to the
same format. Update the .pxd declarations, internal callers, the API
reference template, and the tests to match. (ntips is intentionally
left unchanged.)

* DOC: add dedicated pages for BPTree.shear and collapse

Add the :toctree: option to the "Tree manipulation" autosummary block in
the BPTree class template so shear and collapse each render as a
dedicated API page, consistent with the other BPTree method groups and
with the TreeNode reference.

* API: hide BPTree newick/jplace IO, conversion, and placement helpers

The BPTree backend currently re-exports its newick/jplace parsing and
writing, TreeNode conversion, and jplace placement functions from the
public skbio.tree namespace. These are being set aside while the BPTree
API is reworked, so remove them from the public surface without deleting
the implementations.

- Drop the seven functions from skbio.tree's imports and __all__, and
  delete the "BP input/output and conversion" autosummary block from the
  module docstring so they no longer appear in the rendered docs:
    parse_newick, write_newick, parse_jplace,
    to_skbio_treenode, from_skbio_treenode, to_skbio_treearray,
    insert_fully_resolved
- Keep them importable from the internal skbio.tree.bp subpackage; the
  .pyx sources and the internal _bp_insert -> _bp_conv wiring are
  untouched.
- Redirect the affected tests to import from skbio.tree.bp so the backend
  stays covered.

BPTree and its NumPy .npz read/write methods stay public; that format is
unrelated to newick/jplace and is out of scope here.

* BUG: fix BPTree.read of .npz archives with node names

BPTree.write pickles the object-dtype names array via
np.savez_compressed, but BPTree.read called np.load without
allow_pickle=True, so reading any tree with names raised ValueError
under modern numpy. Pass allow_pickle=True and add round-trip tests
covering the file-like and file-path interfaces (topology, names, and
lengths are preserved).

* MAINT: record the vendored BitArray license

* DOC: add CHANGELOG entry for the BPTree backend

* API: turn BPTree/TreeNode conversions into class methods

The BPTree<->TreeNode conversions were free functions in
skbio/tree/bp/_bp_conv.pyx (to_skbio_treenode, from_skbio_treenode,
to_skbio_treearray). Per PR review, expose them as methods on the
respective classes instead.

Following the reviewers' guidance, provide a single ``from_*`` class
constructor for each direction rather than mirroring ``to_*``/``from_*``
on both classes. ``from_bptree`` is preferred over ``to_treenode``: it
builds via ``cls`` and therefore preserves TreeNode subclasses, and a
paired ``to_``/``from_`` API couples the two classes and complicates
maintenance.

  to_skbio_treenode   -> TreeNode.from_bptree()   (classonlymethod)
  from_skbio_treenode -> BPTree.from_treenode()   (classmethod)
  to_skbio_treearray  -> BPTree.to_array()

The BP->TreeNode build loop lives in TreeNode.from_bptree and constructs
nodes with ``cls`` so subclasses are preserved; BPTree.from_treenode
already builds with ``cls``. BPTree.to_array (an array export mirroring
TreeNode.to_array) is retained.

Delete _bp_conv.pyx and its setup.py extension entry, update the internal
caller in _bp_insert.pyx, drop the removed names from the bp package
exports, repoint the tests to the new methods (with added coverage for
subclass preservation), and document the methods in the BPTree and
TreeNode API reference templates.

* MAINT: defer BPTree jplace placement/insertion to a follow-up PR

Per PR review, the phylogenetic placement/insertion code is being set
aside for a dedicated follow-up rather than landing in the BPTree
backend PR. The design is unresolved: whether placement should return a
BPTree or operate in TreeNode-land, where it should live given skbio has
no placement framework, and how multifurcation and duckdb-miint fit in.

Remove skbio/tree/bp/_bp_insert.pyx (insert_fully_resolved and its
helpers), its extension entry in setup.py, its export from the
skbio.tree.bp package, the test module, and the data/300 jplace fixtures
(also dropped from package-data).

insert_fully_resolved had no consumers besides its own test and was
already absent from the top-level public API, so nothing else is
affected. The jplace parser (parse_jplace) is unchanged and remains a
standalone reader covered by the IO tests.

* API: harmonize BPTree node-count naming with TreeNode

BPTree exposed subtree_size(i) (node count in a subtree) and ntips()
(whole-tree tip count). Per PR review, both correspond to TreeNode.count,
so consolidate them into a single method mirroring TreeNode.count's
``tips`` flag:

  subtree_size(i)  -> count(i)
  ntips()          -> count(tips=True)

count(self, i=0, tips=False) returns the number of nodes (or tips, when
tips=True) in the subtree rooted at node i. The index defaults to the
root (0), so count() and count(tips=True) operate on the whole tree,
matching tree.count() / tree.count(tips=True). Counting tips within an
arbitrary subtree, count(i, tips=True), is newly supported.

Update the internal callers (to_array, __repr__), the .pxd declaration,
the tests, and the API reference rubric.

* MAINT: standardize BPTree Cython headers and tidy imports

Cython-hygiene fixes raised in PR review:

* Add the scikit-bio copyright/license block to the Cython declaration
  files _bp.pxd, _ba.pxd, and _bp_binary_tree.pxd, matching the .pyx
  files. _bp_binary_tree.pxd keeps its upstream (jfuentess/sea2015)
  attribution below the block.

* Apply the project's standard compiler-directive header
  (language_level=3, boundscheck=False, wraparound=False, cdivision=True)
  to _bp.pyx, _bp_io.pyx, and _ba.pyx, matching skbio/tree/_c_nj.pyx,
  _c_me.pyx, and skbio/alignment/_cutils.pyx. None of the BP modules set
  language_level before. cdivision is meaningful for _bp.pyx and
  _bp_binary_tree.pxd (both do integer division in nogil hot paths) and
  inert but harmless for the rest. _bp_binary_tree.pxd's three directive
  lines are consolidated onto one, and test_bp_cy.pyx gains
  language_level=3.

* Tidy _ba.pyx imports: it uses no NumPy C-API, so drop the unused
  `cimport numpy as cnp` and `cnp.import_array()`; import only the needed
  libc functions (`from libc.stdlib cimport malloc, free`, matching the
  `from libc.<mod> cimport ...` style used elsewhere in skbio); and drop
  the unused `Py_INCREF`/`Py_DECREF` from the cpython cimport.

* BUG: validate BPTree topology is balanced

BPTree.__cinit__ checked the balanced-parentheses invariant with an
`assert`, which is stripped under `python -O` — an unbalanced topology
array could then be constructed and cause crashes or incorrect results
later. Replace the assert with an explicit `ValueError`, using integer
arithmetic (2 * opens == length) instead of float division, and add a
regression test.

* MAINT: correct BitArray extern decls and drop trailing commas

Fixes from PR review of the vendored BitArray Cython bindings:

* _ba.pxd declared `uint64_t` as `unsigned int`, so Cython modelled
  `bit_index_t` as 32-bit and its Python->C conversions could truncate
  large bit indices. Declare it as `unsigned long long` to match the
  real 64-bit type (the C storage was already 64-bit, so this is a
  conversion-layer correctness fix with no runtime change).

* The `bit_array_not` extern declaration took three arguments but the
  header (`bit_array.h`) declares `bit_array_not(BIT_ARRAY* dest, const
  BIT_ARRAY* src)`. Correct it to two arguments. The function is not
  called anywhere, so this only fixes the declaration.

* Remove trailing commas from two `cdef:` declaration lines in
  `parse_jplace` (_bp_io.pyx).

* DOC: warn about allow_pickle in BPTree.read

BPTree.read uses numpy.load with allow_pickle=True to restore the
object-dtype names array, which means reading an untrusted .npz file can
execute arbitrary code. Add a Warnings section to the docstring so users
are aware of the risk. Documentation only; behavior is unchanged.

* TST: run BP Cython tests under the test runner

test_bp.py executed test_bp_cy's cdef-level test functions in a
module-level loop that ran at import time, which can make pytest/unittest
collection fail with an ImportError and can run the tests more than once.
Wrap the loop in a TestCase method (BPCythonTests.test_cython_level),
using subTest per function, so the 23 Cython-level tests run under the
test runner instead of during import.

* MAINT: type local variables in BPTree.from_treenode and to_array

Address review feedback on PR #2498: the conversion helpers used
untyped Python locals. Add cdef declarations so the index/counter
variables are SIZE_t/Py_ssize_t and the working arrays are
buffer-typed ndarrays, moving the hot loops to the C level. Also
cache data.sum() in to_array instead of recomputing it.

* PERF: Optimization to BPTree range-excess queries and widen its search kernel to 64-bit (#2541)

* PERF: make BPTree rmq/rMq (and lca/height/deepest_node) O(log n)

`rmq`/`rMq` previously scanned every position in [i, j] to find the leftmost
minimum/maximum excess, an O(span) cost that made `lca`, `height`, and
`deepest_node` linear in the distance between nodes -- and, on large trees,
slower than the equivalent `TreeNode` walk.

Answer the range-minimum/maximum excess query with the rmM (min-max) tree that
already backs `fwdsearch`/`bwdsearch`: scan only the two partial end-blocks and
cover the full interior blocks with a clamped segment-tree recursion over the
tree's internal nodes (`_rmq_tree_min`/`_rmq_tree_max`). The leftmost position
attaining that value is then recovered with a single `fwdsearch`, so the exact
leftmost-tie-break semantics are preserved.

Results are identical to the linear scan (52 BP unit tests; 10.4M brute-force
oracle comparisons over randomized trees covering power-of-2 and non-power-of-2
block layouts and partial tail blocks; 31,773 validate-gate checks -- all 0
failures). The queried span no longer matters: on million-tip trees `rmq`/`rMq`
and `lca` on distant nodes drop from ~6.8 ms to well under 1 us (thousands-fold),
`deepest_node`/`height` on deep subtrees similarly, while near-neighbor queries,
construction, and memory footprint are unchanged.

Refs #2498

* MAINT: widen BPTree rmM/search kernel indices from 32-bit to 64-bit

The rmM (min-max) tree construction and the fwdsearch/bwdsearch/scan_block
search kernel operated on 32-bit C int parenthesis positions, block sizes,
and excess deltas, inherited verbatim from improved-octo-waddle. Because a
position indexes B[0, 2n), this silently capped BPTree at 2**31 parentheses
(~537M tips): beyond it, signed overflow yields negative indices and, under
boundscheck=False, out-of-bounds reads -- corrupt navigation, not a clean
error. The structure this implements (Cordova & Navarro, TCS 2016) assumes a
word-RAM model with w = Theta(log n)-bit words, so no such fixed ceiling is
inherent to the design.

Widen to SIZE_t (npy_intp): the mM.rmm B_size parameter and its
position/loop/excess locals; the block-size field mM.b (so block-index *
block-size products, which are positions, are evaluated in 64-bit); the rank
scan bounds; scan_block_forward/backward positions and bounds; the
fwdsearch/bwdsearch excess-delta d and result; and the module-level min/max
helpers. Block/rmM-tree node indices (k, node, and the _rmq_tree bounds) stay
int: they are O(n / (log n log log n)) and remain < 2**31 for any tree that
fits in memory, so the effective ceiling rises to ~35B tips -- far past the
RAM wall. The stored arrays were already SIZE_t, so nothing on-disk/in-memory
grows.

Output is bit-identical (52 BP unit tests; 31,773 BP-vs-TreeNode validate
checks, 0 failures) and there is no runtime or memory regression (caterpillar
1M and 10M tips: construction, near/far lca and rmq, and the 74 B/node
footprint are all unchanged within noise). The >2**31 capability follows from
the widening but is not directly testable here (a 537M-tip tree needs ~40 GB).

Refs #2498

* DOC: changelog for BPTree O(log n) queries and 64-bit search kernel

Refs #2541

* MAINT: replace the custom SIZE_t typedef with the builtin Py_ssize_t

Replace every use of `ctypedef cnp.npy_intp SIZE_t` with the builtin Py_ssize_t across _bp.pyx, _bp.pxd and _bp_binary_tree.pxd, drop the typedef, and remove the now unused `from ._bp cimport SIZE_t`. Same machine type, no behavior change.

* MAINT: use Py_ssize_t for all non-negative BPTree indices

Several block/node indices and counts were still declared as C int while the arrays they index are 64-bit, leaving a latent 2**31 ceiling and mixing widths on the hot path. Widen them to Py_ssize_t:

- the mM rmM-tree fields (n_tip, n_internal, n_total, height, m_idx, M_idx, r_idx);
- the _rmq_tree_min/_rmq_tree_max parameters and the scan_block_* block index, dropping the now-redundant int down-casts at the rmq/rMq call sites and on the pow(2, height) block offsets;
- the remaining loop/index locals in rmm, _set_edges, the rank helper and fwd/bwdsearch.

Also replace the INT_MAX / -INT_MAX range-tree sentinels with PY_SSIZE_T_MAX so the sentinel cannot be reached by a real excess value now that the kernel is 64-bit, and remove a dead `vbar` declaration.

* MAINT: reuse the excess lookup in BPTree.rmq / rMq

Created new local variable for the fixed query of self._e_index[i] when calling rmq and rMq.

* ENH: read and write BPTree via the newick format through skbio.io (#2528)

* ENH: read and write BPTree via the newick format

Register a newick reader and writer for BPTree in skbio.io. Both are thin
adapters over the compiled parse_newick/write_newick in skbio.tree.bp, so that
reading and writing stay fast on trees with millions to billions of nodes and
neither materializes a TreeNode or any per-node intermediary.

Also fix write_newick to emit branch lengths at full precision ('%s' instead of
'%f', which silently rounded small lengths such as 2.5e-7 to zero) and to
terminate the string with a newline, matching TreeNode's writer.

Refs #2498

* ENH: route BPTree.read/write through the skbio.io registry

Make BPTree.read/write delegate to skbio.io with newick as the default
write format, mirroring TreeNode, and convert the npz round-trip tests to
newick round-trips.

Refs #2498

* TST: cover BPTree newick reader and writer

Exercise the registry-backed BPTree newick reader and writer: exact BP
arrays, {N} edge numbers, write round-trips, registry read/sniff, and error
handling.

Refs #2498

* ENH: keep npz serialization as BPTree.to_npz/from_npz

The compressed-NumPy .npz serialization -- previously the BPTree.read and
BPTree.write methods -- is retained under dedicated names now that read/write
route through the skbio.io registry (newick by default). to_npz/from_npz keep
the former logic unchanged: they store topology, names, and branch lengths
(edge numbers are not stored), and from_npz uses numpy.load(allow_pickle=True).

Refs #2498

* DOC: changelog entry for BPTree newick registry I/O

Refs #2498

* MAINT: address review nits on BPTree.write and to_npz

Use self.default_write_format in write() instead of hardcoding "newick" and drop the to_npz docstring's inaccurate claim that the registry write() preserves edge numbers.

* DOC: surface BPTree.to_npz/from_npz in the API docs

List to_npz and from_npz under the Tree IO rubric so the new npz serialization methods render in the generated documentation.

* MAINT: defer newick edge-number support to the jplace PR

Remove the edge-number documentation and the include_edge_nums writer parameter from the newick format layer, and drop the corresponding tests.

* PERF: faster BPTree construction and SkbioObject registration (#2570)

* PERF: build BPTree select index in O(n) instead of O(n log n)

The select index (_k_index_0 / _k_index_1, giving the position of the k-th
close/open, consumed by select) was built with np.unique(np.cumsum(...)),
an O(n log n) sort over two cumulative-rank arrays. It is equivalently the
set of positions where each bit's running count increments -- i.e. the
positions holding that bit, with position 0 always included -- which is a
single O(n) np.flatnonzero pass. The new build is bit-for-bit identical to
the np.unique result (verified across topologies and the degenerate
B[0]=0 case) and leaves the stored arrays, and thus the memory footprint,
unchanged.

Isolated, this cuts the select-index build ~10x (9.5 ms -> 0.95 ms on a
100k-tip tree), roughly 7% of total tree construction; parse_newick and
from_treenode inherit the speedup. No query hot path is touched.

Refs #2498

* DOC: changelog for O(n) BPTree select-index build

Refs #2498

* PERF: speed up TreeNode.from_bptree with a single compiled traversal

TreeNode.from_bptree walked the balanced-parentheses tree from Python,
calling preorder_select/name/length/edge/parent/preorder_rank on the
BPTree once per node -- a Python/C boundary crossing per accessor per
node. Move that traversal into a single compiled pass, the new
BPTree._to_node_arrays, which returns per-node name/length/edge/parent
arrays in preorder (parent = -1 for the root). from_bptree is reduced to
pure-Python TreeNode assembly over those arrays, so it no longer pays the
per-node dispatch tax; TreeNode object creation (which cannot be
submerged) remains the dominant, irreducible cost.

_to_node_arrays is a plain def, so _bp.pxd and the C vtable are unchanged,
and no query or construction hot path is touched (a single new method is
added). Output is byte-identical: 52 BP tests and 31773 BP-vs-TreeNode
validate checks pass, and a same-process A/B produces identical trees.
Construction is ~1.05-1.15x faster across balanced/caterpillar/random from
1e3 to 1e6 tips (weakest, ~1.05x, on random at 1e6, where the TreeNode
assembly floor dominates).

Refs #2498

* ENH: register BPTree as a SkbioObject virtual subclass

Make BPTree a formal member of the scikit-bio class hierarchy so that
isinstance(bp, SkbioObject) is True and it participates like TreeNode and
other public classes. A Cython cdef class cannot subclass a pure-Python ABC
("first base is not an extension type"), and a pure-Python facade would add a
~34 ns/call dispatch tax to every hot-path operation; virtual registration
(SkbioObject.register) gives hierarchy membership at zero runtime and memory
cost while BPTree stays fully compiled. Also add the __str__ required of
scikit-bio objects (a concise summary delegating to __repr__).

Refs #2498

* DOC: reference PR #2570 in the BPTree changelog entries

Fill in the assigned PR number for the O(n) select-index build and the
compiled TreeNode.from_bptree entries (previously #XXXX), and add a Features
entry for BPTree being registered as a SkbioObject.

* ENH: add a jplace format for BPTree and fix BPTree Newick grammar handling (#2568)

* ENH: add a Cython jplace read/write backend

Migrate parse_jplace(data) -> (DataFrame, BPTree) from improved-octo-waddle and
add write_jplace(BPTree, output, ...), which serializes a reference tree as a
jplace document with an empty placements list. Both run in the compiled backend
and reuse parse_newick/write_newick for the {} edge numbers. Export both from
skbio.tree.bp.

* ENH: add JplaceFormatError

Add the jplace format's error type (a FileFormatError subclass), raised when a
jplace document cannot be parsed.

* ENH: add the BPTree-only jplace format to the skbio.io registry

Register a jplace format with a sniffer, a BPTree reader that returns the
reference tree (placement records are dropped -- use parse_jplace to access
them), and a BPTree writer. Wire JplaceFormatError and the format module into
skbio.io.

* TST: cover jplace BPTree read/write and the parse_jplace helper

Cover reading a jplace file into a BPTree (topology, preserved edge numbers,
dropped placements), writing a BPTree back to jplace (tree/edge round-trip,
empty placements, degenerate edge-less tree), sniffer disambiguation, and the
parse_jplace (DataFrame, BPTree) helper. Add direct write_jplace backend tests
to test_bp_io.py, alongside the existing parse_jplace/write_newick coverage.

* DOC: changelog for the jplace format

Record the new BPTree-only jplace read/write support under Features.

* BUG: correct Newick comment, quote, and whitespace handling in the BPTree backend

The compiled BPTree Newick reader/writer mishandled several grammar cases that
the TreeNode reader already handled correctly. Align them (issue #2349):

- `[...]` comments, including nested ones, are stripped before parsing rather
  than corrupting the balanced-parentheses topology or being misread as edge
  numbers.
- Single-quoted labels round-trip: an embedded apostrophe is read as one `'`
  (a doubled `''` is collapsed) and written back doubled, and the name/length
  split is quote-aware.
- Labels containing whitespace or any of `' _ ; , : ( ) [ ]` are quoted on
  write so the output re-parses losslessly.
- Edge numbers are read from `{}` only; `[]` is now treated as a comment.
  `parse_newick` gained a `convert_underscores` option (default True, matching
  the TreeNode reader); the jplace reader opts out so underscores in accession
  labels are preserved. The jplace format docs are updated to match.

* TST: cover BPTree Newick grammar correctness and jplace tree fidelity

Add BPTree newick round-trip tests for ignored/nested comments, embedded
apostrophes, whitespace quoting, and convert_underscores (direct and via the
registry), plus two battery entries exercising comments and quoted labels. Add
jplace tests for underscore-preserving reference trees, comment stripping with
intact `{}` edges, and special-character label round-trips, and update the
square-brace test to assert `[]` is treated as a comment.

* DOC: changelog for BPTree Newick grammar fixes

Record the comment, quote/apostrophe, whitespace-quoting, and
convert_underscores corrections to the compiled BPTree newick reader/writer
under Bug Fixes.

* ENH: route BPTree.read/write through the skbio.io registry descriptors

Replace BPTree's hand-written read/write with the registry Read()/Write()
descriptors, mirroring TreeNode, so their documentation lists the supported
file formats (newick, jplace). Because BPTree is a Cython cdef class whose
type dict is immutable (and whose instances have no __dict__), the stock
descriptors cannot cache the generated methods on the class; small BPTree-local
subclasses (_BPRead/_BPWrite) reuse the base docstring machinery but cache on
the descriptor instance instead.

* BUG: harden the compiled jplace/newick backend against malformed input

- _strip_comments now raises on an unterminated '[' comment instead of
  duplicating the pre-comment text into the returned string.
- parse_jplace validates that the document is a JSON object (a JSON array
  previously raised a TypeError that bypassed the registry's error wrapping)
  and requires the 'version' member, matching the sniffer's criteria.
- write_jplace rejects a string 'fields' argument and enforces that 'fields'
  includes 'edge_num', so the emitted document stays readable by parse_jplace.
- A node token with whitespace before its branch-length ':' now yields a name
  of None rather than an empty string.

* DOC: fix BPTree jplace/newick docs and update the changelog

- Drop the two :func:`skbio.tree.bp.parse_jplace` cross-references from the
  jplace format docstring (the bp submodule is intentionally not exposed, so

  caveat, which the BPTree-only format never surfaces.
- Correct the newick docstring note that claimed convert_underscores does not
  apply to the BPTree reader; it now does (default True), matching TreeNode.
- Update the changelog: reword the jplace entry to not reference parse_jplace
  and note the BPTree.read/write registry-descriptor integration.

* TST: relocate the jplace fixture and consolidate jplace tests

- Move placement.jplace from skbio/tree/tests/bp/data/200/ to the io format
  test data directory, where the jplace format tests live.
- Remove the duplicated jplace parse/write tests from test_bp_io.py (they are
  covered by test_jplace.py), relocating the one stray newick test back into
  NewickTests, and drop the leaked file handles in the old setUp methods.
- Add coverage for the new backend behavior: empty-name normalization and
  unterminated-comment errors (newick), non-object/missing-version parse_jplace

* BUG: read jplace reference tree without the placements table

The jplace reader routed a tree-only read through parse_jplace, which
built and immediately discarded a full placements DataFrame (scaling with
the file) and required every pquery to carry an "n" member. A valid
document whose pqueries use "nm" instead was wrongly rejected.

Parse and validate the top-level JSON in the reader and call parse_newick
on the "tree" member directly, so reading the reference tree neither
depends on the placement encoding nor materializes the discarded table.
The reader keeps the structural contract (all four members required,
matching the sniffer) and type-checks tree/placements/fields so a
present-but-null member raises JplaceFormatError instead of leaking a
TypeError. parse_jplace is hardened the same way for its own callers.

* BUG: make BPTree Newick edge-number parsing quote-aware

The compiled reader detected an edge annotation with a plain "{" in
token check, which also fired inside a single-quoted label. This
mis-parsed a quoted brace as an edge number: parse_newick("('a{3}',c)r;")
stored the name as "'a" with edge 3, and "('a{b}',c)r;" raised while
converting "b" to an integer.

Add _find_edge_curly, which locates the first "{" outside single quotes
(mirroring _find_length_colon for the branch-length ":"), and use it so a
brace inside a quoted label is treated as literal label content. Unquoted
trailing edge annotations such as "name{3}" are unaffected.

* BUG: reject non-unique edge numbers when writing jplace

write_jplace serialized any BPTree, so a tree with no real edge numbers
(e.g. one read from plain Newick, which has 0 on every edge) emitted a
document with duplicate {0} IDs. jplace edge numbers identify placement
locations, so duplicates make that mapping ambiguous.

Require the tree's edge numbers to be unique before writing, raising
ValueError otherwise. The root has no incoming edge and is not numbered in
jplace (it defaults to 0 in a BPTree and can coincide with a real edge 0),
so it is excluded from the check. The registry writer now surfaces the
backend ValueError/TypeError as JplaceFormatError, mirroring the reader.

* ENH: make BPTree a Python class with Cython and Numba batch engines (#2618)

* ENH: make BPTree a Python class with Cython and Numba batch engines

BPTree becomes a pure-Python SkbioObject that owns its arrays, with its
navigation computed by a compiled engine, and gains batch operations that
run on a selectable engine.

Python class and Cython kernel
- The tree's arrays, including the navigation index, are held by the
  Python object; navigation is delegated to a Cython kernel
  (skbio/tree/bp/_bp_cy.pyx, _BPKernel) whose methods are bound onto each
  instance, so bp.parent(i) resolves straight to compiled code (~5 ns over
  a direct call, rather than ~35 ns through a forwarding method).
- The kernel's nogil methods are declared noexcept, which makes
  navigation 2-3x faster.
- The navigation index is built by the compiled builder in one O(n) pass.
- A bool topology array is accepted, viewed as uint8.

Batch operations and engine=
- close_batch, parent_batch, lca_batch and level_ancestor_batch answer an
  array of independent queries in one call, and cophenet computes the
  cophenetic distance matrix, each with engine= ("cython", "numba",
  "fast"). The Cython kernels use OpenMP prange; the Numba kernels
  (skbio/tree/bp/_bp_numba.py) use prange. Both engines run the same
  algorithm and give bit-identical results.
- cophenet walks each tip's ancestors once, filling the contiguous runs of
  tips whose lowest common ancestor is that ancestor: O(n_tips^2) writes
  and no lca search, with a no-multiply formula so every engine agrees to
  the bit.
- Single-node methods keep no engine argument: it would cost every call
  ~8x (21 -> 165 ns), and a Numba call from Python costs ~1 us.

Numba primitives
- Every navigation operation has a Numba primitive, written once in
  define_primitives(jit, jit_inline) and compiled for the CPU at import
  (the leaf primitives inlined) or as device functions of a Numba GPU
  module on first use. Parity with the Cython kernel is tested for every
  operation, including on Numba's CUDA simulator.

engine="fast"
- The two engines run the same algorithm, so "fast" is chosen from the
  build: Cython if it was compiled with OpenMP (as with GCC on Linux),
  else Numba if installed, else Cython. _bp_cy.OPENMP, set from the
  compiler's _OPENMP, reports the build. Measured on an i7-14700HX with
  14 threads, multithreaded Cython is up to 2x faster than Numba on
  close, parent and level_ancestor, ties on cophenet, and compiles
  nothing at the first call, where Numba compiles each kernel (0.5-2 s);
  Numba is ahead only on lca, by 2-25%.

Fixes
- lca(i, i) returned the parent of a tip, and for the root's closing
  parenthesis read one past the end of the topology array. A node is now
  its own lowest common ancestor (at either parenthesis), in the Cython
  kernel and the Numba primitive alike.
- minselect(i, j, q) with q < 1 indexed from the end (Python's negative
  indexing): q = 0 returned the last minimum. It now returns None, as
  for a q beyond the number of minima, matching its Numba primitive.

Removed
- The vendored BitArray C library (skbio/tree/bp/_bitarray, _ba.pyx/.pxd,
  its extension in setup.py, and licenses/bitarray.txt). It held the node
  masks of shear and collapse, which the kernel now builds as NumPy arrays,
  so nothing used it.
- Four helpers of the rmM tree (bt_offset_from_left/right,
  bt_left/right_leaf), unused here and before.

The BPTree documentation page now lists the batch operations and cophenet.

* DOC: changelog for the BPTree compute engines (#2618)

Entries for the Python-class BPTree with its Cython kernel, the batch
operations and engine= (with how "fast" chooses), the noexcept speedups,
and the lca(i, i), minselect(q < 1) and single-node-tree fixes.

* FIX: give the BPTree rmM tree at least two parentheses per block

The block size is ceil(ln(n) * ln(ln(n))), which gives 1 for n = 4: the
two-node tree (()), a root with a single tip. With one parenthesis per
block the backward search misses position 0, so open(2) answered 0 instead
of 1, and everything built on it followed: the root's last_child came back
as none, and the tip's closing parenthesis resolved to the root in
first_child, count, height, is_ancestor, lca and preorder_rank.

The search's in-block scan reaches back into the previous block to catch
closures that span a boundary, which assumes a block holds more than one
parenthesis; Navarro and Sadakane size blocks at Theta(log n). The block
size is now at least 2, which the formula already gives for every n >= 6.
An exhaustive check of all 626 trees of up to 8 nodes finds (()) the only
tree affected, and none after this change.

The reference index builder in test_bp_cy, the oracle for _build_index,
takes the same floor.

* FIX: let lca and is_ancestor name a node by either parenthesis, in any order

Raised in review of #2618 for closing parentheses; checking it found a
worse case nobody had reported.

- lca(i, j) with i > j could return the wrong node, even for opening
  parentheses: lca(z, x) at (7, 1) gave z itself instead of the root, and
  36 of 100 opening-parenthesis pairs in a 10-node tree depended on the
  order. lca_batch hid this by ordering each pair, so bp.lca(7, 1) and
  bp.lca_batch([7], [1]) disagreed.
- Given a closing parenthesis, lca could return a closing parenthesis as
  the answer (88 of 400 open/close combinations in the same tree).
- is_ancestor(close(x), x) was True: a node named by its closing
  parenthesis counted as its own ancestor, though is_ancestor(x, x) is
  documented to be False.

All of these predate this PR. lca now brings both arguments to opening
parentheses in order before its search -- for the usual opening arguments,
two byte tests and a compare -- in the Cython kernel and the Numba
primitive alike, so lca_batch no longer orders its pairs and the public
Numba lca takes them as they come. is_ancestor tests strictly inside the
node's span.

The tests missed it because the batch was checked against the single-node
method, and both run the same kernel. They now use an independent
reference, a stack scan and parent pointers: lca across closing
parentheses and both orders on both engines, and every tree of up to 7
nodes for lca, is_ancestor, close, parent and first/last_child. The Numba
primitive takes reversed pairs, and on the CUDA simulator, unordered ones
over every position.

* FIX: check cophenet's engine before returning early for few tips

Raised in review of #2618. cophenet resolved its engine only after the
early return for fewer than two tips, so cophenet(engine="julia")
succeeded on such a tree but raised on any larger one, and an explicitly
requested but unavailable Numba engine went unnoticed. The engine is now
resolved first, so argument checking does not depend on the input size.

* DOC: changelog for the lca, is_ancestor and two-node-tree fixes

Widens the existing lca(i, i) entry to the argument-order and
closing-parenthesis cases, and adds entries for is_ancestor and for
navigation in the two-node tree (()).

* ENH: GPU-resident BPTree with Numba GPU kernels (#2628)

* ENH: hold BPTree on a GPU and run its batch operations and cophenet there

A BPTree can now be created from a non-NumPy topology array, e.g. a CuPy
array or a PyTorch tensor on a GPU, and with engine="numba" its batch
operations and cophenet run as Numba GPU kernels, on CUDA and ROCm.

Device-resident trees
- The tree keeps the given array as its data and is built from a host copy
  of it (one byte per parenthesis over the bus), so the Cython kernel and
  every existing method work unchanged. New trees and exports (shear,
  collapse, pickling, to_array, to_npz) come from the host copy.
- Batch queries are validated where they are: NumPy queries with NumPy,
  device queries on their device through the array API. Batch results take
  the array backend and device of the queries; cophenet returns its
  DistanceMatrix in those of the tree's data.

GPU kernels (skbio/tree/bp/_bp_gpu.py)
- As in PERMANOVA and Mantel, the GPU is not an engine: engine="numba" on a
  tree whose data is on a CUDA or ROCm device (it exposes
  __cuda_array_interface__) runs the kernels, compiled on first use from
  the single-source device primitives. CPU arrays never initialise a GPU
  driver.
- The tree's index is uploaded once and cached per GPU module. Device
  queries are read in place; host queries are uploaded and the result
  downloaded.
- cophenet runs one block per matrix row, its threads walking the row's
  ancestors together, so every write is along a row and no mirrored pass
  is needed. It is bit-identical to the CPU engines: its formula only swaps
  operands between (a, c) and (c, a), and has no multiply to fuse. One
  thread per element with an lca search each was 5-13x slower.
- A kernel that cannot build or run warns once and falls back to the CPU
  engines. The helpers for this and for choosing the Numba GPU module
  (skbio/tree/bp/_gpu.py) follow those of PERMANOVA and Mantel
  (skbio/stats/distance/_gpu.py), including the preference for
  numba-cuda-mlir, but keep their own record of failed backends, so that a
  BPTree kernel failing does not disable the PERMANOVA and Mantel kernels,
  or the reverse. Unifying the two is left to a later change; this one
  touches nothing outside skbio/tree.
- engine="fast" chooses the GPU for a tree on one the kernels can use,
  and otherwise the CPU rules.
- Numba's warning about the low occupancy of a small grid is filtered on
  these launches: a small batch or tree is a legitimate input.

Measured on an RTX 4070 Laptop GPU against 14-28 Cython or Numba threads
of an i7-14700HX, on 1M-tip trees with the queries on the device: lca_batch
3.2 ns per query against 53 ns (16x), parent/close 0.5 ns against 3.7-5 ns,
level_ancestor 0.8 ns against 8.8-11 ns. With host queries lca keeps an 8x
lead; the cheap operations become transfer-bound. Each GPU call has a fixed
cost of 0.3-0.6 ms, so the GPU overtakes the CPU at 1e4-1e5 queries. cophenet
on 20k tips takes 26-31 ms against 0.43 s (Cython, 14 threads), 0.53 s if
the 3.2 GB matrix is copied to the host; on caterpillar trees it is no
faster than the CPU.

The figures above are with numba-cuda. With numba-cuda-mlir 0.5.4 (NumPy
2.5) a kernel runs within 15% of them (lca_batch 3.8 ns per query against
3.3 ns on the same day), but compiles more slowly: the first lca_batch call
took 9.6 s against 0.8 s, as lca's device functions are the largest.

Tests
- The device tests assert that engine="numba" and "fast" ran the GPU
  kernels on CuPy and PyTorch trees, and the real-device checks of the
  primitives run through the module the dispatch chooses. All are array-API
  tests, so the GPU workflow runs them as it is, and its warning filter
  fails the job when a BPTree kernel falls back.

Not yet tested: ROCm, systems with several GPUs (the default device is
used, as in PERMANOVA), and PyTorch on CUDA outside the GPU workflow.

* DOC: drop machine-specific timings from the BPTree comments and docstrings

Timings measured on one machine do not hold on others, so the comments
and docstrings of the BPTree engines no longer quote them: the cost of
the bound kernel methods, the speed-ups behind the engine="fast" rules,
the GPU crossover batch size, the rejected cophenet kernel layout, and
the cost of Numba's dispatch and of the array-API wrappers. The rules of
engine="fast" are unchanged.

* ENH: add BPTree.to_device to move a tree to a GPU or another array backend

A tree reaches the GPU kernels only if its data is on a GPU, which until
now meant building it again from a device array. A tree read from a file
or converted from a TreeNode had no direct way there.

tree.to_device(xp, device=None) returns the tree with its data copied to
the array backend xp (e.g. cupy, torch, jax.numpy, or numpy for the host)
on device, given in that backend's own terms, as array API namespaces
take it (e.g. "cuda" for PyTorch, a device number or cupy.cuda.Device for
CuPy, or the device of an existing array).

- Nothing is rebuilt: the new tree shares the host copy of the topology,
  its navigation index and the node attributes. Only the topology is
  copied, one byte per parenthesis; on a GPU the index follows at the
  first kernel that needs it, as for any device tree.
- Each tree gets its own compiled kernel object, since set_names,
  set_lengths and set_edges replace the kernel's arrays: setting an
  attribute of one tree does not change the other.
- The construction shared with __init__ moves to _assemble.

* DOC: changelog for the GPU-resident BPTree (#2628)

* FIX: write a GPU-resident BPTree from its host copy

The Newick and jplace writers iterated the tree's data, which for a tree
on a GPU reads one element per parenthesis back from the device. They
now iterate the host copy of the topology that every tree keeps, as the
other host-side operations do. Writing a 100k-tip tree on a GPU took
14 s as Newick and 30 s as jplace; it now takes the 0.18 s and 0.23 s of
the same tree on the host, with the same output.

Reported by Copilot in #2628.

* FIX: wait for the queries' GPU stream before a BPTree kernel reads them

The kernels run on a stream of the Numba GPU module, and read the queries
and write the result of the array's own backend in place. CuPy tells
Numba which stream produced an array (__cuda_array_interface__ version
3), but PyTorch does not (version 2). Work still queued on a PyTorch
stream could therefore be read unfinished: level_ancestor_batch casts
int32 levels after the position range check last synchronized, and on a
non-default stream its kernel read the levels before the cast finished.
With the cast delayed on the stream, 333,676 of 500,000 results were
wrong.

A GPU backend's array is now handed to Numba only after the work queued
on that backend's current stream is done (_gpu._sync_stream, called by
_bp_gpu._on_device for every query and result array), whatever the
backend and the Numba GPU module. This also keeps a result buffer that
PyTorch's caching allocator reuses from being written while queued work
still reads it. The wait costs microseconds against a call's fixed cost.

Tests: the reading order, and level_ancestor_batch, lca_batch and
cophenet on a warmed GPU tree inside a non-default CuPy or PyTorch
stream with int32 queries. On PyTorch the casts are delayed on the
stream, which makes the test fail without the wait (83% of results
wrong). The PyTorch tests ran on CUDA locally.

Reported by Copilot in #2628.

* DOC: update the GPU speed-ups in the changelog to the fixed code (#2628)

* ENH: expose the BPTree navigation to Numba code on the CPU and GPU (#2629)

* ENH: expose the BPTree navigation to Numba code on the CPU and GPU

The new public module skbio.tree.bp.numba gives the navigation operations
of BPTree as functions callable from a user's own compiled code:

    nav = bpn.cpu()          # for @njit code
    gnav = bpn.gpu(cuda)     # device functions, for @cuda.jit / numba.hip

and BPTree.numba_arrays(gpu=None) exports a tree's arrays for them, as
nav.parent(T, i). A per-node method called from Python pays the
interpreter's overhead, far more than the navigation itself, and a GPU
call has a fixed cost of a fraction of a millisecond; the batch methods
amortise that over independent queries only. Inside a compiled loop a
navigation function costs only the operation itself, which is what
computations with dependent steps need (e.g. the lca of each sample's set
of tips, a walk to the root).

- The functions are the compiled primitives the Numba engine already uses,
  restricted to those with a BPTree method of the same name (the index
  operations stay private). They return what the method returns, with its
  sentinels; the differences are documented: -1 for None (a compiled
  function has one return type, and a GPU device function cannot return an
  optional value), a boolean for is_tip and is_ancestor, and count's
  positional tips argument. The documentation also warns that a sentinel
  passed on to another function does not fail but answers for another
  node (-1 indexes from the end, and 0 is the root). It also warns that a
  kernel can read a PyTorch tensor before PyTorch's stream has written it
  (its __cuda_array_interface__ carries no stream), as #2628 found for the
  batch operations, and shows how to wait for the stream.
- T is the topology and index only, which cannot change for a tree's
  lifetime: read-only views on the host, uploaded once and cached on the
  tree on a GPU. Node attributes, which set_lengths/set_edges replace, are
  passed separately through new read-only lengths and edges properties.
- tip_positions() and positions(names) map between names and the
  positions kernels work in; positions resolves a name as TreeNode.find
  does (a tip first). cophenet shares that lookup, and checks its
  endpoints for duplicates with a set rather than a list.
- Numba stays optional: the module imports without it, and cpu()/gpu()
  raise ImportError.

The module documentation lists Navigation, and its examples run as
written, the GPU one including the transfer of the kernel's arrays and its
launch configuration.

On the documented workload, the lca of each of 100,000 samples of 1-20
tips on random trees of 1K-1M tips (i7-14700HX, RTX 4070 Laptop GPU,
numba-cuda-mlir), the kernel is 9-13x faster than a Python loop over
bp.lca on 14 threads and 2.2-2.9x faster than reducing padded samples with
lca_batch; on the GPU it is a further 10-20x faster with the data on the
device (1.1-2.6 ms), and 6-7x with host data transferred on every call.
T costs no host memory, and 37-40 bytes per node on a GPU.

Tests cover the helpers, every public function against its method, the
documented kernels written at module level as a user would, and the GPU
example on the CUDA simulator and (with SKBIO_DEVICE=cuda) a real device.
There, every function but level_next is also compiled into a kernel and
checked against the CPU's. level_next's forward search reads one element
past the end of the rmM tree when it starts in the last block, which the
simulator's bounds checks reject; that index issue is fixed separately,
and level_next is tested on the CPU here. A tree on a GPU, created from a device array or moved there
with to_device, gives its positions and attributes as NumPy arrays on the
host, and its numba_arrays(gpu=...) is uploaded once and shared with the
batch operations.

* DOC: changelog for the BPTree Numba API (#2629)

* FIX: BPTree forward search past the rmM tree, and preorder_select ranks from 1 (#2632)

* FIX: stop a BPTree forward search at the last rmM leaf instead of reading past it

fwdsearch climbs the range min-max tree from the block it starts in,
checking the right sibling of each left child on the way. The leaves are
stored up to the last block only, so when the last block is a left child
its right sibling is one past the end of m and M, and the internal nodes
right of the last leaf are stored but empty. A search that starts in the
last block and finds nothing there, e.g. level_next of the root or of a
node on the right edge of the tree, read past the end of the arrays.

The results were right, but the read is undefined, and in a GPU kernel it
can fault. Nothing lies after the last block, so a search that starts
there and finds nothing in it now returns -1 before climbing, in the
Cython kernel and in the Numba primitive. That one comparison suffices: a
search from an earlier block meets the sibling holding the last leaf
before any empty node, and that sibling's range always includes the final
excess of 0, which is the only excess the zeros of an empty node match.
The index is unchanged.

The check is outside the climb's loop because a check on every level, the
first version of this fix, made the GPU lca kernel 11-19% slower (lca
reaches fwdsearch through rmq). In an interleaved A/B (4 rounds, lca of
100,000 samples of 1-20 tips, 10K and 1M tips), this version is within
noise of the code without the fix on every engine, CPU and GPU.

The CUDA simulator, which checks bounds, found it while running every
Navigation function in a GPU kernel. A bounds-checked sweep of the Numba
primitives (NUMBA_BOUNDSCHECK=1) over 366 random and caterpillar trees
found 4,238 such reads, all in fwdsearch from the last block, and finds
none with the fix; fwdsearch also matches a brute-force search at every
position and offset of those trees. The new test runs fwdsearch as Python, where NumPy
checks every index, and fails without the fix.

level_next is back in the GPU test of every Navigation function, which
left it out for this reason.

The defect came with the port from improved-octo-waddle.

* FIX: count BPTree preorder_select ranks from 1, as preorder_rank does

preorder_rank counts from 1 (the root is 1), but preorder_select counted
from 0, so it was not the inverse its documentation said: given a node's
rank, it returned the next node in preorder, and for the last node it read
past the end of the select index. postorder_rank and postorder_select both
count from 1.

The cause was the layout of the select index, inherited from
improved-octo-waddle, which built it as
np.unique(np.cumsum(...), return_index=True). A tree starts with "(", so
the running count of closing parentheses starts at 0, and that 0 became a
leading entry of their index: select(0, k) counted from 1. The count of
opening parentheses starts at 1, so their index had no such entry and
select(1, k) counted from 0. Later rewrites kept the arrays bit-for-bit,
and the tests encoded the difference ("needed +t on expectation, unclear
at this time why").

The index now holds the positions of each parenthesis in order, with no
leading entry, and select(t, k) is the k-th occurrence for either
parenthesis, counting from 1, in the Cython kernel and the Numba
primitive. preorder_select now counts from 1, and to_node_arrays and
collapse_mask, its two internal callers, pass i + 1, as to_array already
did for postorder_select. postorder_select is unchanged otherwise.

Both selects now return -1 for a rank outside 1 to the number of nodes,
rather than read outside the index: a rank of 0, as callers used before,
would otherwise give an arbitrary position. The Numba preorder_select
does so without a branch (it clamps the rank, then masks the result): a
branch made it too large for LLVM to inline where it is called through
the Navigation tuple, and the call that remained, passing T, made it
21-36x slower. postorder_select calls open and was never inlined, so its
check costs nothing measurable.
Like the other single-node methods, they do not raise, being bound
directly to the compiled kernel. -1 is the sentinel the methods already use
for "no such node" (parent of the root, and minselect in the Numba
functions). The documentation gives the ranks' range, with examples, and
the GPU test of every Navigation function now uses ranks from 1, plus 0
and n + 1.

select is the only reader of the index arrays, and preorder_select and
postorder_select its only callers. The index is never saved (pickling and
to_npz keep the topology and rebuild it). Outputs that rely on select are
identical before and after on 11 trees of 1 to 5,000 nodes: to_array,
TreeNode.from_bptree, the node arrays, collapse, shear, Newick, jplace,
pickling and cophenet. A new test checks that both selects invert their
ranks for every node and return -1 for any other rank, and a
bounds-checked sweep of the Numba primitives, with ranks out of range
included, finds no read outside the index.

* DOC: changelog for the BPTree index fixes (#2632)

* FIX: accept unsigned 64-bit ranks in the Numba BPTree preorder_select

The branch-free clamp of preorder_select, min(max(k, 1), T.size // 2),
mixes the rank with signed integers. For an unsigned 64-bit rank, Numba
types min and max of uint64 and int64 as float64, so select indexed with a
float, and a kernel calling nav.preorder_select with uint64 ranks failed
to compile (TypingError). It compiled before the clamp, and
postorder_select, whose check is a comparison, still did.

The rank is now made signed (np.intp) before the clamp. Every integer
dtype gives the nodes the int64 ranks give, and an unsigned rank beyond
the signed range, which becomes negative, gives -1 like any other rank
outside 1 to the number of nodes. Found in review.

A new test runs both selects in a compiled kernel with int32, uint32,
uint64 and intp ranks and with ranks of 2^63 and above, and fails without
the fix; the GPU test of every Navigation function repeats the selects
with uint64 ranks (compiled on a real device; the CUDA simulator does not
type the code, so it cannot catch this).

* BUG: BPTree Newick reader crashes and mislabelling, apostrophes, and edge numbers in pickles (#2634)

* FIX: parse Newick tips without labels, and quotes, in BPTree without overflowing

parse_newick wrote the parentheses into a buffer of len(data) bytes with no
bounds checks, but a tip without a label writes two parentheses for at most
one character (',' or ')'). Valid Newick overflowed the heap: "(,);" wrote
6 bytes into 4 and failed as unbalanced, and "(" + "," * 1000 + ");"
segfaulted. Its second pass, which assigns labels, advanced only on labels,
so a tip without one was not counted and the labels after it went to the
wrong nodes: "(,b);" named the first tip b. These inputs crashed before, so
this was not seen.

The tokenizer took '"' as a quote, while the rest of the parser and the
TreeNode reader take only single quotes. A double quote inside a quoted
label, or an unclosed quote, swallowed the final ';', and the tokenizer then
returned an uninitialised index: "(a\"b,c);", "('a\"b',c);" and
"(a,b)'x;" segfaulted, and a tree with a node named 5" could not be read
back after writing.

parse_newick now makes one pass over the tokens, writing the parentheses and
the node metadata together. Each '(' and ',' starts a child, and a child
that does not start with '(' is a tip, with a label or not. The arrays are
sized exactly from a count of '(' and ',' outside quotes, every write is
checked against that size, and input that is not a single tree (unbalanced
parentheses or quotes, a second top-level node) raises ValueError. A double
quote is an ordinary character, as for TreeNode. The tree is built once,
with its names, lengths and edges, rather than built and then updated.

Checked against TreeNode.read, for the topology and every name, on 3,000
random trees in which some labels are missing; on 3,000 random trees in which
every tip is labelled (quoted labels, comments, edge numbers, line breaks),
the parentheses, names, lengths, edges and errors equal the old parser's.
300,000 random mutations of Newick strings either parse into a valid tree or
raise ValueError, with no crash. Parsing a 1M-tip tree takes the same time
(median ratio 0.99 over 9 alternating rounds in fresh processes) and leaves
the same resident memory (248 MB).

* FIX: keep the edge numbers of a BPTree in pickles and copies

__reduce__ passed the parentheses, lengths and names, but not the edge
numbers, so pickle.loads, copy.copy and copy.deepcopy returned a tree with
every edge 0 and no edge lookup: edge_from_number raised TypeError, and
write_jplace rejected the copy for duplicate edge numbers. It now passes the
edges when the tree has an edge lookup, so a copy of a tree without edge
numbers has none either, as before. Pickles written before load as before.

* FIX: read apostrophes in BPTree Newick labels as the TreeNode reader does

BPTree collapsed '' to an apostrophe only inside a fully quoted label, and
took the quotes of any other label literally, while the TreeNode reader
treats '' as an apostrophe anywhere: its writer escapes an apostrophe as
'' without quoting a label that needs no quotes otherwise. So a file
gave different names as a BPTree and as a TreeNode: a tip named O'Brien,
written by TreeNode as O''Brien, read back as O''Brien in BPTree, a label
written '' (the name ') read as None, and a label quoted in part, e.g.
a_'b', kept its quotes and had its underscore converted.

_unquote_name now follows the TreeNode reader: each quote opens or closes a
quoted part and is dropped, a quote right after a dropped one is kept, and
underscores become spaces unless convert_underscores is off or the label
ends with a quote closing a quoted part. The structure was already found
that way, as every quote toggles the quoting. One quirk of the TreeNode
reader is not copied: it reads a quoted space as a space and an
apostrophe, as it skips whitespace when looking for the quote before; here
a space is a character like any other. Unquoted whitespace inside a label,
which the TreeNode reader rejects, is still kept.

The writer now handles apostrophes as the TreeNode writer does: it doubles
them whether the name is quoted or not, and no longer quotes a name for an
apostrophe alone (O'Brien is written O''Brien, as by TreeNode). Under the
TreeNode reading, a quoted name made of apostrophes only (the name of one
apostrophe, quoted, is four quotes) would read back with one apostrophe
too many.

Tests: eight labels with apostrophes and underscores, quoted in whole, in
part and not at all, give the names, lengths and topology of
TreeNode.read; names with apostrophes and underscores written by TreeNode
read back the same in BPTree, and written back by BPTree, in TreeNode. The
test of the registry writer now expects O''Brien unquoted. Checked beyond
the tests: 10,070 random labels of a, _ and quotes that TreeNode reads give
the same names in BPTree (none differ), and 4,820 random names with
apostrophes, underscores, spaces, commas and colons written by BPTree read
back the same in BPTree; TreeNode reads them too except where it cannot
read its own writer's output for the name either. The 3,000-string corpus
of earlier commits parses as before, and parsing a 1M-tip tree takes the
same time (1.002x over 6 alternating rounds in fresh processes) and
memory. Found in review.

* DOC: add the changelog entries of the BPTree Newick reader fixes

* BUG: BPTree navigation at positions and topologies outside a single tree (#2635)

* FIX: stop BPTree.shear looping forever on a single-node tree

shear_mask walks from each kept tip up to the root, stopping at position 0,
but the parent of the root is -1. In a single-node tree the root is the only
tip, so the walk started at -1: it wrote to the byte before the mask, and
looped forever, as the parent of -1 is again -1. Single-node trees can be
built since #2618. The walk now stops at any position up to 0.

* FIX: return -1 from BPTree navigation for a position outside the tree

The navigation methods of the Cython kernel, which BPTree binds directly,
did not check their positions. first_child, last_child, next_sibling,
previous_sibling and preorder_rank handle a closing parenthesis by calling
themselves on open(i), and open(i) returns i for i <= 0, so a -1 whose
preceding byte was 0 recursed forever: bp.first_child(bp.parent(0)) and
bp.preorder_rank(bp.preorder_select(0)) hung. -1 is the sentinel that parent
returns for the root, and that preorder_select and postorder_select return
for a rank outside the tree since #2632. The other methods read outside the
tree's arrays for such a position: bp.depth(-1) returned whatever preceded
the excess array.

Each navigation method now returns -1 for a position outside 0 to
data.size - 1 (is_tip and is_ancestor return False) before reading
anything, with one unsigned comparison. A -1 passed from one method to
another thus gives -1 again. The BPTree notes say so, and the Numba
functions' warning, which do not check their arguments, points to the
difference. name, length and edge index a NumPy array and are unchanged.

* FIX: reject a BPTree topology that is not a single tree

The constructor checked only that half the parentheses were opening ones.
It accepted bytes other than 0 and 1, a closing parenthesis before its
opening one, and several trees in a row, and the navigation, which assumes
a single tree, then read outside the tree's arrays: BPTree([2, 0, 0, 0])
had a select index of one entry for two nodes, BPTree([0, 1, 1, 0])
.last_child(0) read B[-1], and BPTree([1, 0, 0, 1]).first_child(3) read
B[4]. The forest [1, 0, 1, 0] was accepted silently.

The constructor now also checks that every byte is 0 or 1, and that the
root closes at the last position, naming the first position at fault.
build_index finds where the root closes in its pass over the excess, at
the first position where the excess drops below 1, so the check adds no
pass over the index. to_device reuses the tree's checked arrays.

* FIX: let a BPTree backward search from position 1 find position 0

bwdsearch(i, d) finds the nearest position before i whose excess is
excess(i) + d. Its block scan returned -1 early when the last position to
scan was 0 (`if upper_bound <= 0`), so a search from i = 1 never found
position 0, although its scans from other positions of the first block do
include it. In the Cython kernel and the Numba primitive alike. No current
caller asks for that target (open, enclose and level_ancestor search from
1 for an excess that position 0 cannot have), so no result was wrong, but
the index operation was, for any new caller.

The early return is removed: the scan's range is empty when nothing lies
left of i in the block, and stops above lower_bound >= -1, so it reads
nothing outside the array. It removes a branch rather than adding one.

A new test compares both searches of both engines with a brute-force
search, for every position and every reachable excess of trees of up to
43 rmM blocks, running the Numba primitive as Python so that every read is
bounds-checked; it fails without the fix (24 mismatches over the test
topologies, all from i = 1, in both engines). fwdsearch had none.

* FIX: return -1 from the BPTree Numba functions for a position outside the tree

The functions of skbio.tree.bp.numba did not check their positions, as
documented: a position outside [0, T.size) read outside the tree's arrays,
which on a GPU can fault and leave the device unusable, and -1, the
sentinel of parent and of the selects, indexed from the end, so
nav.depth(T, nav.parent(T, 0)) returned the excess at the last position.
The Cython methods return -1 for such a position since the previous
commits, so the two engines disagreed.

Every Navigation function taking positions now returns -1 for a position
outside the tree (is_tip and is_ancestor return False), as the methods
do; mincount and minselect too. Each primitive checks its positions
itself, with one comparison before anything is read, rather than through
a wrapper around the primitives. preorder_select and postorder_select
already returned -1 for a rank outside the tree.

Tests: the public functions return -1 (False) for positions -n, -2, -1, n
and n + 1, alone and in pairs, matching the methods, and a sentinel passed
on gives -1 again; the GPU test of every Navigation function, compiled into
a kernel, now includes such positions and pairs, on a real device (CuPy
with numba-cuda and numba-cuda-mlir, a…
